name: FatePreview
tagline: A rules-based tool for mapping out the branches of a real-life decision and comparing their trade-offs.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The product is self-described as deterministic: fixed planning rules in, structured comparison out, no model weights and no proprietary corpus. That is a decision tree plus a scoring rubric plus a decent reading experience, which an agent can assemble in a single sitting. The genuinely hard part of this category is not the code, it is writing prompts that make you think clearly, and you can lift that structure from any decision-making framework in a library book. What you give up is the polish: the tidy layout, the sensible default question set, the feeling that something impartial is looking at your life. If you are willing to author your own criteria and weights, a local build does the same job and keeps the contents of your midlife crisis off someone else's server.
coreLoopDIY: Enter a decision, define options and weighted criteria plus hard constraints, and get a deterministic side-by-side comparison with flagged trade-offs and generated next steps you can export.
requirements: Willingness to write your own criteria, weights and constraint rules
Nothing else: no API keys, no accounts
whatYouLose: A curated default question set built by someone who has thought about decision framing for longer than you have
Polished presentation that makes the output feel considered rather than like a spreadsheet
Any sense of external impartiality; your DIY version only knows the weights you gave it
Mobile-friendly access across devices without you hosting anything
Whatever scenario templates and guided flows ship with the paid product
moatNotes: The rules are the product and rules are copyable. What is not trivially copyable is the editorial judgment in which questions get asked and in what order.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the value is not the arithmetic, it is being walked through a structure you would never impose on yourself. Opening a blank file and inventing your own criteria and weights is exactly the work people pay to avoid, and a tool that hands you the frame already filled in gets you to a usable answer in ten minutes instead of an hour of staring. There is also a quiet psychological element: output from a thing you did not build feels less like you rigging the result, even when the math is identical.
notes: A weighted scoring model with good manners. The honest test is whether you will actually fill it in.
prompt:
Build a local-first decision comparison tool as a single-page web app. No backend, no accounts, no telemetry, no AI API calls.

Stack, non-negotiable: Vite + React + TypeScript, Tailwind for styling, Zustand for state, localStorage for persistence. No router beyond simple in-app view state.

Core data model:
- Decision: title, context note, created date.
- Option: label, description, optional cost field, optional time-horizon field.
- Criterion: label, weight 1 to 5, direction (higher-is-better or lower-is-better).
- Constraint: label, type (hard or soft), and a per-option pass/fail or value check.
- Score: per option, per criterion, integer 0 to 10, entered by the user.

Behavior, all deterministic, no randomness anywhere:
- Weighted score per option = sum(score * weight) / sum(weights * 10), shown as a percentage.
- Any option failing a hard constraint is marked Excluded and visually separated, never silently dropped.
- Soft constraint failures render as warning chips on the option card.
- Trade-off view: for the top two options, list every criterion where they differ by 3 or more points, phrased as 'Choosing A costs you X on criterion, gains you Y on criterion'.
- Sensitivity check: recompute rankings with each criterion's weight set to 1, and flag any criterion whose weight alone flips the top ranking. Label those 'this decision hinges on how much you care about ___'.
- Next steps: for the top option, auto-generate a checklist from its unresolved soft constraints and from any criterion scored 4 or below, as 'Verify ___ before committing'.

UI: three views, Setup (decision, options, criteria, constraints), Score (a grid of options by criteria with number inputs), Review (rankings, trade-offs, sensitivity flags, next steps).

Ship with two seeded example decisions, 'Take the job offer or stay' and 'Move cities or renew the lease', each with criteria and constraints prefilled so the app is usable on first load.

Add Export: download the full decision as Markdown, and Import: paste that Markdown back. JSON export too.

Explicitly out of scope: predictions, probabilities, confidence intervals, any language implying the app knows the future, multi-user sync, auth, hosted storage.

Include a README with run instructions and one paragraph stating plainly that this is a structured scoring tool and the output is only as good as the weights entered. No .env is needed; do not add one.
